summary: Specifies the Time Zone Information Format (TZif), a file format for representing and exchanging time zone information independent of any particular service or protocol. It also defines two media types for the format. It was replaced by RFC 9636.

plainLanguage.summary: A file format that holds the rules for what time it is in each place, including when clocks jump for daylight saving time. Programs read it to show the right local time.

questions: how does tzif store timezone transitions
subtitle: Binary file format for representing time zone information and rules.

tldr.problem: Systems need a standard way to store and exchange time zone information including UTC offsets, daylight saving transitions, and leap-second adjustments.
tldr.mechanism: TZif defines a binary format with a header, data blocks for 32-bit and 64-bit timestamps, time zone designations, and a footer containing POSIX TZ rules for times beyond the transition table.
tldr.outcome: The format was standardized and is widely used on UNIX systems and for time zone data distribution, though it has been superseded by RFC 9636 which extends it further.

today: RFC 8536 is an Internet Standard and remains in active use. Time zone information is widely distributed in TZif format through the IANA time zone database and via TZDIST services. It has been superseded by RFC 9636 which clarifies and extends the format further.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Time Zone Information Format (TZif) is a binary format used to represent time zone data. Time zone information includes UTC offsets, daylight saving time rules, local time designations (abbreviations), and optional leap-second adjustments.

TZif was introduced in the 1980s and is the format used by most UNIX systems and the widely deployed IANA time zone database. This document provides the first formal standardization of the format's structure, supporting versions 1, 2, and 3, each offering greater time range and flexibility than the previous version.
sections.plainLanguage: TZif is a file format, like a ZIP or PDF, that holds all the timezone rules for a place: what it is called, how many hours from UTC, and when daylight saving time happens.

sections.title: File Structure and Versions
sections.content:
A TZif file is divided into logical sections. Version 1 files contain a header and one data block. Version 2 and 3 files extend this with a second header and data block (using 64-bit timestamps), followed by a footer.

The version field in the header indicates the format version. Version 1 (NUL) uses 32-bit transition times limited to 1901-2038. Version 2 ('2') adds 64-bit transitions, allowing any date. Version 3 ('3') is like version 2 but allows extended TZ string syntax for complex rules.

All multi-byte values are stored in network byte order (big-endian). The version 1 data block is included in versions 2 and 3 for backward compatibility with old readers.
sections.plainLanguage: The file is like a book with chapters: version 1 data (old format), then version 2+ data (new format with far-future dates), then a rule string for times beyond the table.

sections.title: Binary Format Details
sections.content:
Each TZif header is 44 octets and contains:

Magic and version: A 4-byte ASCII "TZif" identifier followed by a version byte (NUL, '2', or '3').

Counters: Four-byte unsigned integers for the number of UT indicators (isutcnt), standard/wall indicators (isstdcnt), leap-second records (leapcnt), transition times (timecnt), local time types (typecnt, must be at least 1), and time zone designation octets (charcnt, must be nonzero).

The data block contains transition times (sorted UNIX timestamps), transition type indices, local time type records (6 bytes each, containing UTC offset, DST flag, and designation index), time zone designation strings, and leap-second records.

A local time type specifies the UTC offset (in seconds), whether DST is in effect, and which time zone abbreviation to use. For example, EST is -18000 seconds (5 hours west), and EDT is -14400 seconds (4 hours west).

The footer (versions 2+) contains a newline, an optional POSIX TZ string, and a closing newline. This rule string defines local time for dates beyond the last transition in the table.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is like a table with columns: when time changes happened (in seconds since 1970), what timezone abbreviation to use (EST, EDT, etc), and how many hours from UTC.

sections.title: Time Zone Data Distribution
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how TZif files are used with the Time Zone Data Distribution Service (TZDIST), defined in RFC 7808. A TZDIST server can deliver time zone data in TZif format, indicating support via the application/tzif or application/tzif-leap media types.

application/tzif indicates the file contains no leap-second records, while application/tzif-leap indicates leap-second data is included. Systems can truncate TZif files to specific date ranges for efficiency; a truncated file remains valid for timestamps within the truncation bounds.

TZDIST clients request TZif format via the HTTP Accept header and can rely on receiving consistent, versioned time zone data from the server.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer asks a server for timezone information, it can request the data in TZif format, and the server sends the binary file. Servers can trim the file to just the years the computer cares about.

sections.title: Security and Integrity
sections.content:
TZif files contain no executable code and no extensible areas for malicious data. However, when processing TZif data, implementations must check all count fields to prevent buffer overflows or reads past the file end.

TZif provides no built-in confidentiality or integrity protection. Time zone information is typically public, so confidentiality is not usually needed. However, transmission of time zone data can leak location information (past, present, or future). When sent over public networks, TZif data MUST be protected with a confidentiality layer such as TLS. For critical systems, external integrity protection (digital signatures) may be necessary, as the format stores no integrity metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: The file format itself is safe, but if someone intercepts it, they could see where someone is or was by the timezone. So it should be sent through an encrypted connection, and in important systems, should be digitally signed.
